utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there was one preliminary matter the Prosecution would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Your Honours, yesterday according to my records, the Prosecution exhausted its allotment of 200 hours to present its case. This morning I make an application pursuant to Rule 73 bis subparagraph (f) for the time necessary to lead the evidence of our last witness, Reynaud Theunens. Rule 73 bis states that the Trial Chamber may grant this request if satisfied that doing so is in the interests of justice. A great deal has changed since the Prosecution submitted its original estimate of 200 hours on the 10th of February 2012. We have found it necessary to both add and drop witnesses, respond to decisions by both the Trial and Appeals Chamber, and adapt to defences as they have been revealed over the course of the trial. I have at all times sought to adapt our case presentation to remain within our original estimate, and I believe we have consistently demonstrated the value the Prosecution places on the efficient use of our time. I submit that it is in the interests of justice to afford the Prosecution the time necessary to lead the evidence of Reynaud Theunens in light of all of the circumstances, including developments in the case, the Prosecution's efficient use of time to date, and the importance of Mr. Theunens's evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Stojanovic, any response.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our position is, Your Honours, that we will not oppose this Prosecution initiative, although, as per our records, and what we've seen so far, I believe that the credit of 200 hours has already been breached a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any further submissions, especially in relation to the claim that you have used your 200 hours already a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think that's incorrect, Your Honour. The Registrar's report last Friday, I believe it was 199 hours and 11 minutes we had used in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I believe it has been the practice in this Tribunal that redirect also goes towards the time of the Prosecution case in chief, in which case we are well over 200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we revisit the pre-trial conference, the Prosecution in its estimate said that it would take 200 hours for its direct examination, and the Chamber in its pre-trial conference indicated that it would agree or it condoned or approved that. There was never any -- I mean, how would the Prosecution ever estimate the amount of re-direct it would require for its case? We only know that once we are in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we leave the matter of examination-in-chief, whether or not that we have to add for the 200 hours the re-examination, because the Defence doesn't oppose. So, therefore, we leave that alone for the time being. We're not going to verify that at this very moment. Leave is granted to present the evidence of Mr. Theunens, if that goes beyond the 200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other matter? If not, I -- Mr. Groome, you announced, and I am referring to the Prosecution's notice of disclosure of expert reports of Patrick Treanor, pursuant to Rule 94 bis dated the 25th of September. You announced that you would rely only on a -- not on all the paragraphs but on specific portions of the reports. They're set out in paragraph 1 of this notice, and the Chamber would like to receive a redacted version of the reports only presenting the paragraphs, the portion that the Prosecution wants to rely upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. We'll provide the redacted portion. Our intent was to take a similar approach to the one that we did with Dean Manning's report in that we did not redact the entire report. We allowed it -- we didn't darken it out so that it could be viewed for evaluation of professionalism, credibility, all of those things, but made it clear that we were only relying on those paragraphs, so we'll abide by the Court's direction either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. If there's nothing else, is the Defence ready to continue its cross-examination, Mr. Stojanovic, of Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor can be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Treanor, I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we stopped while we were discussing the mandate and the authorities of the National Security Council. Let's take a look at P3003, in e-court, paragraph 267. Would you please clarify certain things written in that paragraph. While waiting for the page to be retrieved, let me remind you that you discussed that the National Security Council comprised of -- inter alia, one military personnel, who was, at the time, carrying out the duties of the minister of defence. Let me now focus your attention to a portion of your report where you state, it will be third sentence in this paragraph: "On the 15th of April, the security -- National Security Council appointed Bogdan Subotic, member of the SNB, minister of defence, as acting commander of the TO. On the 22nd of April, the SNB decided that Radovan Karadzic should co-ordinate commanding the TO forces." My question to you is: Until what time the command and control of the TO worked in the territories under the control of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by "under the control of the assembly." The assembly, as we've seen yesterday, basically converted the -- the TO into the army of the Serbian republic on the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the command over the Territorial Defence from the 15th of April to the 12th of May was in the hands of General Bogdan Subotic as member of the National Security Council?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my impression from the documentation I've seen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you agree with me that, in practical terms, until the 12th of May, 1992, General Ratko Mladic had no command authority in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at a certain point in time, I -- I believe in early May, he was appointed the deputy commander of the 5th Military District. I believe that's mentioned in -- in the addendum, the exact dates. So I believe that that was his first entry, so to speak, into the Bosnian scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that that military district was under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army as the federal army?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, then, that until the 12th of May, 1992, General Ratko Mladic had no authority concerning the Territorial Defence which is discussed in your -- in paragraph 267 of your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- the Territorial Defence, within the framework of the -- the Yugoslav defence system, could co-operate and indeed operate under the command of the JNA, and indeed I believe JNA units could theoretically operate under the command of TO commander depending on the situations in any particular region. I won't go into the background of their defence doctrine. And I believe that at the beginning of April 1992, Dr. Karadzic as president of the National Security Council gave a directive, and I believe one of the points in that directive was related to the co-operation, if not subordination, of TO units to JNA units in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether in your report you established whether the moment when General Mladic is given specific duties in the JNA within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? When was that moment?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I -- I believe it is mentioned in the -- at least in the addendum, the date of his appointment. I -- I -- I don't -- I can't remember the date offhand, and I don't know exactly where it is in the report -- in the addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, at any point in time - and we -- this date was the 9th of May 1992 until the 12th of May 1992, when he was formally appointed as commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. Did you mentioned, noticed, or found any document in your analysis which would reflect General Mladic's superior position over the Territorial Defence units as commanded by General Subotic at the time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall any such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the last sentence of your report where you state -- I mean your -- this paragraph of your report, where you state: "On the 13th of July," therefore after the VRS had been established and the -- and the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina had been established, "Presidency decided to place the reserve police under the unified civilian military command which was controlled by the Presidency as the Supreme Commander of the army." Professor, what do you mean by civilian military command with respect to reserve police?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you direct me to a particular paragraph? I thought we were discussing paragraph 267, but I ... oh, yes, I see it now, 267. It's not the last sentence. Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's the last sentence of paragraph 267.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's been -- in my addition, it's the second-to-last sentence. I see it now. Well, that wording comes from the decree. I -- I -- they mean what -- they mean what they mean. I haven't added any meaning to that. If you're asking me what does that mean, I would say that that means the -- under the command of the Presidency, who was -- which was in charge of civilian affairs as well as military affairs. Under the terms of the defence law, the president of the republic during an imminent threat of war was in command of the police forces and was always in command of the military forces so that -- that's the unified civilian military command, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we agreed that on the 15th of April, the decision was taken to declare imminent threat of war and it was established -- published in the Official Gazette on the 15th of May, 1992. Would such wording reflect that, since 12th of May 1992, the Presidency was the only body authorised to command reserve police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object as to the question. Actually, the transcript from yesterday at T 20185, line 19, involved the issue of the 15th of April 1992 declaration which -- and Dr. Treanor was asked: [As read] "When was the decision on proclaiming an immediate threat of war issued?" His answer was: [As read] "It was issued on the 15th of April, 1992." Mr. Stojanovic responded: [As read] "Professor, the decision was made one month later in May 1992. Was this a mistake or do you have some specific knowledge regarding when it was published as opposed to when it was made? When did it enter into force?" And the witness -- Dr. Treanor answered: [As read] "Well, my recollection is that it was -- the decision was taken on the 15th of April and entered into force on that date. It was published in the Official Gazette, so it would be easy to consult that." That seems to be a different conversation than is reflected in the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, Ms. Bibles took you to that portion of yesterday's transcript where the witness said we can verify when it was published in the Official Gazette and that he apparently did not agree with the suggestion that it was only on the 15th of May but he left that open. Now, in your question, you presented as an agreed fact. That means you and the witness that it was on the 15th of May. Could you either rephrase your question or explain why you diverted from yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I fully accept that portion of what the witness said yesterday. The decision on declaring an imminent threat of war was taken by the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 15th of April, 1992, and it was published and confirmed by the Assembly of the Serbian people in BH by publication in Official Gazette number 6, 12th to 17th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the proper way of phrasing the question would have been that you agreed yesterday on the decision to be taken on the 15th of April and that the Defence's position is that that was published on the 15th of May. That would have been the proper phrasing of the question. I think the witness has not answered any question yet. Could you please repeat or pose the question in relation to this decision and its date of publication, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall, Your Honours, with your leave. Let's take 65 ter 0712 -- 07212, because I don't believe that this is contentious.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, let's go -- we will get back to this question but let us first clarify this point beyond doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, a portion of the English translation of this decision has been blackened out. This decision concerning the declaration of an imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But let me ask you, Professor, shall we agree that the decision on declaring an imminent threat of war was taken by the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 15th of April, 1992? And that it was ratified by the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina on a session on the 12th of May, 1992, and published in the Official Gazette, number 6, for the period 12th to 17th May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can't read the -- the English because it's not there, and I -- I can't read the Serbian because it's too small. But I'll take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there's no agreement -- is there any -- Ms. Bibles, is there any dispute about the -- the publication date?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As to the publication date, no. The effective date of the declaration is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we see the top of the B/C/S page and ... there we see a date of 12th to 17th May 1992. Whatever that means. Perhaps we can see the next page in English. Especially the top of the page. No, there's no date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I see -- Mr. Stojanovic, is it your position that the decision preceding the decision 143, as we can see it on our screens, that that is the decision by which the imminent threat of war was declared?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in the B/C/S, we can see that decision number 142 - I'm -- cannot read it but at least it reads "odluka" which I understand is decision. Reference is made to both the 15th of April and a little bit further down, the 12th of May. Is that what you are referring to? And perhaps we could enlarge it for Mr. Treanor, the original in B/C/S. Could we first go to the left of that page so that we can see what it is. 141. Then, again, to the right of that page. Can you read this, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can now, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 142. Could you tell us whether this is the decision that you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it have the date of the decision as the 15th of April under number 03-11/92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it say below that that it is published on the 12th of May, with a reference to that same number, and, again, the date of the 15th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it -- it says that on 12th of May the -- the Assembly of the Serbian People confirmed that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it was published in the 12th to 17th of May, 1992, number 6 Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, to assist this process, perhaps if we went to 65 ter 19144, I believe we would find the accurate English transcript for this declaration. And I -- I throw that out to assist counsel in getting a clear record on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could have a look at it, although it seems that -- that there's no disagreement about the matter. One second, please. Yes, there it seems to be -- Mr. Stojanovic, next time it would save a lot of time if you would choose the 65 ter number which specifically addresses this decision we find under number 142 in the Official Gazette of the 12th to 17th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we zoom in, please, on that translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, let us now have a look at the following document. It's a 65 ter document, 02462. These are the minutes from the 24th Session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The date is 6th of August, 1992. And let's have a look at page 2. It's page 2 in both the B/C/S version and in the English version. And on that page we can see the conclusions. And it says that: [As read] "The Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and the date is 6th of August, "states in its conclusions we will activate the work of the commission for investigating war crimes committed against the Serbian people even if it is necessary to replace the members of the commission." And now have a look at the second paragraph or the next paragraph where it says that: [As read] "We'll consider the attitude adopted towards prisoners of war who are in prisons in Serbian territory. The prisoners should be categorised into three's groups: Those who were captured at the front line, those who armed and assisted TO actions, the actions of the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and those who assisted and financed Alija's army. It was pointed out that we should abide by international conventions when treating prisoners of war, when dealing with prisoners of war." And then in the final sentence, it is says: [As read] "To this end, we suggest the prisoners of war be treated in a totally humane manner because they in prisons, not in concentration camps. They are being provided with food, clothes, hygiene, they're being protected at our expense in war time." So the Presidency says: [As read] "An order will be issued -- the Ministry of Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina will be ordered to examine its municipal branches -- through its municipal branches the behaviour of all civilian authorities and individuals guarding prisoners of war. The information will be passed to the MUP which will pass it on to the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." This is the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Professor, if we have a look at these minutes from the session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who was in charge of these facilities which were used to detain prisoners in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that point in time? Who supervised these facilities and who was in charge of them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are two questions. Could you please make a distinction between who was in charge and who supervised facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: First I will ask you who was responsible for the overall procedure that had to do with prisoners of war? I'm referring to the supervision of these prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that is a -- a complex issue. I'm under the impression on the basis of orders that Minister of Defence Bogdan Subotic issued pursuant, I believe, to instructions from the Presidency in May or June 1992 which were published in the gazette, that prisoners of war were subject to the Ministry of Defence. However, there were people in detention who were held by civilian authorities or, indeed, perhaps even by private individuals, people who had no -- no official position as well. And I believe the -- the last paragraph of this, the instruction to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, relates to that, to look into these people that were being held by civilian authorities and individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I hear that your typing is going through the microphone of Mr. Stojanovic, and we see that you're busy and zealous. That's great. But perhaps you could organise it in such a way that it doesn't reach our ears. We'll only read your writings at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps see the first page of the English translation of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, could this document be admitted into evidence. It's a 65 ter document; 02462 is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02462 receives number D443, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And, finally, could we have a look at the 65 ter document 02461.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, it is a session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was held one day earlier, on the 5th of August, 1992. And I'm interested in the first page. Please have a look at the fifth paragraph under item 1 where it says that the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 5th of August, 1992, examined the following. And here it says as far as certain military formations are concerned, and in brackets says brigades, which are in the territory of Banja Luka but are not under military command, they should be placed under unified military command and they should be withdrawn from Banja Luka. Professor, in the course of your work, did you have any contact with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stojanovic. Can you tell us where you are reading exactly? You said fifth paragraph under item 1. I'm not quite sure what -- where that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's the sixth paragraph, but the paragraphs start in -- in a different way. But can we zoom in on the English translation. The paragraph starts with: "Regarding individual military units ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 6, I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the original text, that's what I'm reading from: [As read] "As far as individual military formations are concerned, (brigades) which are in the territory of Banja Luka but are not under military command, they should be placed under unified military command and withdrawn from Banja Luka. They should be withdrawn from Banja Luka." The question is whether you, in the course of your work and when analysing the work of the Presidency, found out anything about what is at stake here. Which military formations were not placed under military command in Banja Luka? And the date was the 5th of August 1992; I'd like to remind you of that fact.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I really can't recall anything about -- further about that circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, did you have any information obtained from the documents that you examined which indicated that certain paramilitary formations existed in the territory of Krajina and in the Banja Luka surroundings and were not under the immediate control of the VRS in the middle of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I certainly do recall documents discussing the issue of so-called paramilitary organisations or units; but, again, I'm sorry, I really can't recall anything related to Banja Luka, in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the 65 ter document 02461 please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02461 receives number D444, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to conclude, but could the document 1D01478 also be admitted. It's amendment 62 to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Because I believe that we used this document yesterday and there was a translation, and then there is something else I would like to say in relation to three other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, any objection against admission amendment 62?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01478 receives number D445, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And as you suggested yesterday, Your Honours, I suggest, together with the Prosecution, that by the end of this week, we should agree on the relevant provisions of the SFRY constitution used under 65 ter 07482 and the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was used in this court under 65 ter document 17211, and after we have agreed about the relevant provisions, the Defence is interested in, and the Prosecution as well, then we could suggest that these two documents be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any selection made of documents, such as the constitution, should be uploaded anew so that we only receive in evidence the selected portions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have already decided what we will use in relation to these two documents, and if there is nothing contentious we can come to agreement with the Prosecution if there's anything they want to make use of. We'll read out what we want to make use of. It concerns the SFRY constitution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please upload the selected portions on which you agree with the Prosecution. We'll then decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honours. Thank you. I have now dealt with the documents I wanted to tender. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I understand that that's -- concludes your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Ms. Bibles, I don't know how much time you would need. If it would be more than five to seven minutes, I would suggest that we take an early break. If, however, you can deal with the matters in a short time, then you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just estimating my time somewhere between ten and 15 minutes. So perhaps a quick break would be -- or an early break would be in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We first take the break now. We first ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness can be escorted into the courtroom. I put on the record that Judge Fluegge is unable to continue to hear the case for urgent reasons. That will be of a short duration; actually, only for the remainder of this day. And Judge Moloto and I have decided that it's in the interests to continue to hear the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, just for your information, the Chamber will hear -- hear the remainder of your testimony in the absence of Judge Fluegge. Ms. Bibles, if you're ready to re-examine the witness, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: First, with respect to 15 April 1992 declaration, I do have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could see 65 ter 0474 on our screens. This would be the minutes, the joint session of National Security Council dated 15th April 1992. I'm sorry, Your Honours, I'll have to come back to this document and move on to a different document. If we could see 65 ter 02864 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: First, could you tell us what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this appears to be a document communicating decisions to local authorities in the Serbian republic from --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from the -- it's sent by the Ministry of Defence of the Serbian republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And could you tell us the date of this decision?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the date of the document is 16 April 1992, and it conveys one decision that was made at a session on --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, directing your attention to decision 2.1 at the bottom of the first page in English, and I believe it's also on the first page in the original version, could you describe for us what it -- whether this assists you in understanding the effectiveness or the effective date of the declaration of imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. This is the -- at the bottom of the page, under the second heading where it says "decision," point 2 says -- is it point 2 --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- you're interested in? General public mobilisation has been ordered on the territory --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Actually, I'm sorry, point 1.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Bibles apparently you were referring to 2.1 --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but the 2 doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the second decision displayed on this page under number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That's exact. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. Point 1 states a state of imminent threat of war has been declared, although the word "state" does not appear in the original B/C/S. It apparently says "an imminent threat of war."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And also, we may need to look at the rest of the document, you were questioned on cross-examination regarding the subordination of the TO to the JNA. I'll ask that we look at the second page of this document and see if this document assists in understanding that question further as well.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, under point 4 it says that war units -- do not withdraw from war units the mobilised units that have been attached to JNA formations, which would imply that TO units had been attached to JNA formations and would remain attached to them. The next point says with the remaining TO formations, mobilise regular number of men and materiel and equipment with which the territory can be secured and the possibility of surprises prevented. So I guess it's just the first paragraph that would be relevant to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 02864.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, right at the very end, I haven't seen this document in a while, it says: "In preparing the instructions as well as the engagement of TO units, achieve co-operation with JNA units and where possible put them under single command."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02864 receives number P3027, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at a decree, decree number 250 of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, dated 25 April 1992, and it says that: [As read] "... utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES

utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And Your Honours, finally, I would tender the document used on cross-examination 19144 which was the declaration with the correct English translation, the 15 April 1992 declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, Ms. Bibles. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19144 receives number D446, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D446 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are documents that we'd seek to admit from the bar table following this witness's testimony. However, since Mr. Stojanovic and I will be meeting with respect to the constitution issues, perhaps we could go through the documents at that same time and then meet back with the Chamber later this week with a list that we would agree to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no objections in itself. But if you do not reach any agreement, we need the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm satisfied with the testimony so far with respect to the bar table documents at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any idea about the number you wish to tender from the bar table?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We have -- my quick review, I believe it's about 20 documents right now.

utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed as you suggested, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES

utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. They stay as previously expressed.

utterances.text: 3003 and 3004, Your Honours.

utterances.text: Before we do so, Ms. Bibles, I think I earlier instructed you and, indeed, slightly different from what we did in Manning's way, you asked for some background information to be kept. However, in relation to these report, also looking at the balance background and report itself, before we finally decide on admission, and therefore, when I said "is admitted into evidence," we -- I withdraw that and we should wait for the redacted versions to be uploaded and then we'll decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we also have that as true as 3003 and 3004. And then I think P3008 is still MFI'd. That is, the decree on the promulgation of the National Defence Act, 28th February 1992, signed by Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I believe that was the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the -- the one where -- okay. That's -- but that is now admitted as a D exhibit, or is that -- that was --

utterances.text: I believe this is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now let me see, before I get ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P3008 was the document in which Mr. Treanor identified a flaw where we asked it to be verified by CLSS. That has been done. And is there any -- is there a new translation or has CLSS confirmed the accuracy of the translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not have the new translation yet. We will advise the parties and upload that version when it comes available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then P3008 remains MFI'd. My apologies for mixing up the two translation issues. Have the questions in re-examination triggered any need for further questions, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, Your Honours, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Further cross-examination by Mr. Stojanovic:

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, we revisited the decision on proclaiming an imminent threat of war which the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued on the 15th of April 1992, and the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina confirmed that on the 12th of May, 1992. My question is: At which point would such a decision enter into force? On the day of its adoption by the Presidency, on the day of its confirmation by the assembly, or on the day of its publication in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe it would come into force on the day of its adoption. These were, that and other designations, were taken pursuant from emergency powers. It's -- it's in the nature of emergency powers that things have to be done immediately. It would be absurd to take a decision and give people instructions but say don't do anything until it's been confirmed by the assembly when the situation that has arisen was one that dictated immediate action in the absence of the assemblies. So I think it came into effect immediately on the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me that this decision fell within the purview of the assembly and that only in exceptional cases the powers of the assembly would be taken over by the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And the decision was taken on the basis of those emergency powers of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. One additional question. The fact that that decision was sent out, does that also underlie your opinion that it took immediate effect? Because we've seen on the 16th of April it was at least sent to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and apparently received in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. It was something that had to be acted on immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And was acted upon --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions. Mr. Treanor, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to this -- to -- to the two courtrooms and having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's always a pleasure to assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, would you take care to upload the -- both the Treanor reports after having been redacted by this Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And, Your Honour, the courtroom is filling up on our side. May I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are excused. Before we'll invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, I'd like to deal with a few matters, a few procedural matters. One is directly linked to the next witness. In relation to the documents to be used with Expert Witness Theunens, the Chamber would like to, once again, address the matter of documents to be used with Expert Witness Theunens. In the latest exhibit list for this witness, the Prosecution indicates that it intends to use approximately 20 documents during the examination. However, in a submission of the 23rd of September of this year, the Prosecution requested the Chamber to pre-assign exhibit numbers for 895 documents that it, at the time, intended to use with the witness. On the 25th of the September, the Chamber denied this request and asked the Prosecution to review the exhibit list in light of the Chamber's guidance of the 29th of October, 2012. This guidance can be found on transcript pages 4138 and 4139. On the 9th of October, 2013, the Prosecution informally communicated that although it had proposed to tender about 500 documents with "the remaining expert witnesses," it now intended to tender these documents in a bar table motion. On the 17th of October of this year, the Chamber addressed this matter, and in this respect, I refer the parties to transcript pages 18022 through 18025, and I will not repeat the Chamber's statement now. The Chamber notes that on the 31st of October, 2013, the Prosecution submitted a bar table motion including, inter alia, 434 military/residual documents. The Chamber understands that a large part of these documents are, in fact, documents underlying the Theunens's report, and therefore documents that the Prosecution initially intended to tendered with this witness. In accordance with the guidance given on the 17th of October, 2013, the Chamber strongly urges the Prosecution to tender those -- these documents during the examination of Witness Theunens, provided that, as the guidance reads, they concern, and I quote "matters of central importance to its case which are likely to be controversial and which require further explanation, clarification, or illustration in terms of how the expert witness reached his or her conclusions or opinions." Further, if the Defence challenges Witness Theunens's conclusions, and the Defence is under an obligation to do so, and the Chamber expects it to do be done during cross-examination of the witness, the Chamber then expects the Prosecution to tender the related documents immediately. Meaning, if challenged through cross-examination, in re-examination. And earlier, the Prosecution said that it might need further time to know exactly what to tender. If there's any need for such additional time, then the Prosecution can address the Chamber. The Chamber hereby instructs the Prosecution to review the bar table motion of the 31st of October, 2013, within one week from the last day of Witness Theunens's testimony. It should exclude from the motion those documents that have been tendered through this witness and file a notification to this extent. This is the further guidance by the Chamber. Mr. Weber, I see that you're on your feet and are dying to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: First of all, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just on a couple of points that the Chamber raised. Thank you, we understand the comments that the Chamber provided. I would just note though that our recent notification, we indicated that the Prosecution may use any documents that are referenced in the Theunens report and then added the additional 20 or so that you said are not referenced in the Theunens report. So it wasn't our intent, nor do I believe does our recent notice indicate, that we are limiting it to just 20 documents. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you slow down a bit, then our transcriber would appreciate that I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So of course we will endeavour to use documents that underlie the report during the course of the examination. The second note, and this is just something for the Chamber's consideration, but it has also struck me during the course of my preparations: The Chamber's guidance or inclination that was expressed on the 25th of September, 2013, instructed the Prosecution to lead any relevant matters from part 1 of the report. Now, in actuality part 1 of the report constitutes a very much lower quantity of documents than part 2 of the report, which is actually quite heavy in terms of the quantity of documents. Many of the documents that overlap, as Your Honour has observed, with the recent bar table motion come from part 2 of the report. So there's a -- a logistical time element where in preparations it's also been something that has quite struck me that the Chamber's guidance in one way is asking me to present evidence related to part 1 and, of course, Your Honours, I'm willing and happy to do so, and yet in another way, the Chamber's guidance is restricting the amount of documents that can be tendered with respect to another thing. And as we've said multiple times through submissions, these documents are quite relevant to our case. So I appreciate Your Honours' guidance and I understand it, and I'd also -- we'll see as it progresses through the examination, but I'd kindly request if maybe the Chamber could also consider that aspect of the circumstances that we face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you said that you have multiple times submitted that these documents are quite relevant to your case. I understand that because they're underlying the report of Mr. Theunens and what Mr. Theunens says about them is relevant. Now, the issue is where do we rely on Mr. Theunens having reviewed material which is footnoted and rely on Mr. Theunens's observations and conclusions, and where there is a challenge to this footnote material, the underlying documents, to justify the conclusions. If there's no such challenge, we just are satisfied with the report. If there is a challenge, and, again, I repeat, that, of course, the Defence, when the witness is here, should put those documents to the witness, should challenge that these documents - at least if that's their position - if they challenge the conclusions, then, of course, it becomes more important for the Chamber to form its own opinion to what extent those underlying documents justify the conclusions drawn. That is the issue. So that they are relevant is fully understood. That relevance appears from the reports. To look into further detail in those materials becomes important once there is a challenge by the Defence. That is the basic thought behind the Chamber's -- behind the Chamber's guidance. Now, if you intend to say that they're relevant, these documents, beyond what is found in the report, then there is the more reason to put them to Mr. Theunens because otherwise we would not know, where Mr. Theunens used those documents, why they are relevant in other aspects. In another respect, that is the reason why we urged you that if it needs further explanation or if you consider them to be relevant for the report -- beyond the report of Mr. Theunens, to -- to explain that because we are not aware of it. We see the same documents underlying the Theunens report appearing in the bar table submission, where we earlier said, we do not -- it's our guidance not to tender underlying documents where the Theunens reports deal with the materials in those underlying documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand the Chamber's position. The Prosecution does have some additional views on that, but I believe that I understand your position to the extent that if I need to revisit it during the course of the testimony and how time develops, if the Chamber would indulge me at that time to maybe make some additional comments on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll then hear from you. Then a matter unrelated -- yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification so I can understand the procedure precisely. Originally you had said if the Defence challenges conclusions, the Prosecution should tender the relevant documents in re-direct examination. But now at temporary transcript page 32, there seems to be an indication that the Defence has to -- has to put those documents to the witness and tender the documents. Is it on the Defence or on the Prosecution to tender the documents if they're used?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What should be done, if you raise the issue, whether Mr. Theunens does draw conclusions which cannot be based on the underlying documents, then if you tender them in order to demonstrate why the conclusions are not justified on the basis of those documents, of course, then there's no need for the Prosecution to do it any further. If you just, without tendering the documents, put questions to Mr. Theunens which clearly come down to a challenge of his conclusions, then, of course, the Prosecution, being aware of that, is -- I wouldn't say invited, but would have to consider whether to tender the underlying documents so as for the Chamber, later, to rely upon in assessing whether the conclusions were justified or were not justified. So it depends a bit on the practice the Defence will develop in challenging the conclusions of Mr. Theunens. If that includes the tendering -- I mean, important is that if you challenge the conclusions that you put to Mr. Theunens on what that challenge is based. And I would say that in 80 per cent of the cases, you would need to put the document to the witness, which, I then take it, it is in the interests of the Defence, then, to have that document to be admitted into evidence. So it is a practicality rather than a matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there are a few other matters -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have two other matters which the Chamber would like to raise before we are running out of time later today or in the days to come. The first one is the Chamber's thoughts on the further scheduling of this case, a matter which was raised also by the Defence. Having received and considered the submissions from the parties last week, the Chamber would like to share with the parties its initial assessment of the further scheduling in this case. The Prosecution's last witness will be heard this and probably next week. The Defence indicated that it would need six months from this point in time -- and, of course, all this on the assumption that if a 98 bis motion would be filed, that it would be denied so as to -- because otherwise there's no need to present a Defence case at all. Six months, as said, was needed. Considering that there is still a number of unknown factors such as when the Chamber will deliver its last evidentiary decision in the Prosecution's case, and the possible re-opening of the Prosecution's case, but, apart from that, as matters stand now, the Chamber is inclined to set the start of the presentation of any Defence evidence at the 13th of May, 2014. The Chamber will issue a Scheduling Order in due course with its final decision on when any Defence evidence shall be presented. And this concludes the Chamber's statement on this matter. For the next item, I'd like to briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. In order to start the -- hearing the testimony of the next witness with a clean slate, I have one more matter which is not that urgent but relatively short as well. It deals with P2508 which was MFI'd with Witness Andreas Riedlmayer. On the 17th of October of this year, the Prosecution tendered P2508 into evidence. It indicated that the document, consisting of transcripts of a Bosnian Serb Assembly session of the 23rd of August, 1993, might be the subject of an agreement with the Defence. I refer to transcript page 17998. The Chamber notes that the document was not part of the Prosecution's bar table motion of the 31st of October, 2013, dealing with evidence related to the Bosnian Serb Assembly. The Chamber understands that there's no agreement between the parties concerning P2508. Considering the very limited portion used with Witness Riedlmayer - I think it was only one page - the Prosecution is instructed to redact P2508 accordingly. And the Chamber would like to hear from the Defence its position on the admission of P2508. I can imagine that you're not immediately prepared to give that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I believe that my colleague Mr. Lukic handled that witness, so we would like to consult with him since he's not in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we hear from you this Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That deals with all the procedural matters I had in stock. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I think that the transcript does not reveal any further secrets, so the curtains of the public gallery can be open again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I refer to "the transcript," I meant the transcript as visible on the Prosecution screens, visible from the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Theunens. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Theunens. Mr. Theunens, you'll first be examined by Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber is, as you know already very likely, he's counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Reynaud Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time, could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 03975.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Exhibit P2368, under seal. I apologise. It's 039.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now -- I'm now wondering what will appear on our screens. Madam Registrar, was -- what appears on our screen now is a curriculum vitae and that's the -- so, therefore, it's not an exhibit under seal but that was an error. Yes. utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, this is the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel kindly speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, there is the curriculum vitae that you provided the Office of the Prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I mean, I can add it's old because it doesn't include my current occupations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could just ask you to look under section 2, it indicates that you received a bachelor degree in social and military sciences at the Royal Academy in Brussels. Could you please briefly tell us what this degree entails.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, actually, I mean, I'm a bit surprised we used this CV because at that time, this was in the transformation, what I have is [French spoken], which is actually equal to a masters degree, and I think I corrected that in the subsequent CVs I handed over to the ICTY. utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under section 4, you indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, before we continue with this one, are there other differences? Because it might have been better to use the most recent and corrected one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of and this is the one that we have in our possession. I was just going to ask him at the end just to update his current position which is the only thing that I am aware is missing from this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, but also the translation of the degree. I mean, in the English there's a difference between a bachelor and a masters obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, the Chamber would prefer to check that you verify that and that we hear the evidence of Mr. Theunens even in the absence of having looked at his CV in further detail at this very moment. You could still revisit any updated or old CVs once you have verified which is the most adequate one to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I can continue with asking the questions based on the information in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under section 4 of this CV, you indicate that between September 1992 and June 2001, you were employed by the Belgian Ministry of Defence, military intelligence and security service. Could you please describe what your duties were during this time.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, my duties are as described in the CV. I mean, to summarise I worked as an analyst on the Balkans that focussed on monitoring and analysing and preparing assessments on the political and military developments in the Balkans at that time. That was focused on areas where Belgian troops deployed, i.e., Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, but obviously it also included monitoring these events in other parts of the Balkans, i.e., Serbia and Montenegro and to a much lesser extent FYROM Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you participate in UN peacekeeping operations in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours. To summarise the CV, between December 1994 and May 1999 I spent approximately 25 months in the Balkans. First of all, November 1994 till October 1995 as a military information officer in the UNPROFOR/UNPF headquarters in Zagreb. And then subsequently from June 1996, I think, until May 1997, as a military information officer in the UNTAES headquarters in Vukovar. And my last assignment was from December 1998 till, I think it was again, May 1999 as a chief of a national intelligence cell in the SFOR headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: According to your CV, you worked as part of the military analyst team of the Office of the Prosecutor from 2001 onwards. During this time, did your research an analysis cover the activities of various military and paramilitary formations that were involved in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That -- that is correct, Your Honours, and I left the OTP in April 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Since April 2009, how have you been employed?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, since April -- actually, end of April 2009, I'm chief of the joint mission analysis centre in the United Nations interim force in Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And could you please generally tell us what your duties entail in your current position.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am in charge of what is called integrated team, i.e., consisting of military and civilian personnel, who -- whose task it is to monitor and analyse developments within the area of responsibility of -- of UNIFIL as well as Lebanon as well as the region developments that may be relevant for mandate implementation, and the mandate being determined by United Nations Security Council Resolution 1701 of August 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will come back to the CV issue later during the examination. However, at this time, could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 28612.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, did you author the report before you which is entitled: "Ratko Mladic and the JNA 2nd MD-VRS (1992-1995)," which is dated September 2012?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of your own report with you here today?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have you placed tabs and made highlights in your copy of the report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I did, just to facilitate my testimony, i.e., to identify specific parts in an easier fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 15 of both versions of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention to paragraphs 3 and 4 of the scope and methodology section of your report. In these paragraphs, you refer to the intelligence cycle method of analysis. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what this analysis entails.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, just a small correction: The intelligence cycle is more like a research method, and analysis is a step or a phase in the intelligence cycle. But basically the intelligence cycle consists of four discreet phases, they are discreet because they influence each other. You start with direction, i.e., have you to identify what do I want to research. Based on that, you will gather information, the so-called collection phase. It's not sufficient just to gather information, but then have you to process that. Process is actually in the -- in the terminology of the intelligence cycle consists of transforming information into intelligence whereby the big difference, I would say, between information and intelligence is you have subjected to your judgement. And the last phase of the intelligence a cycle consists of dissemination; i.e., you are going to make the findings or the product of your analysis available, and in this particular case that consists of a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one moment. While I do not objection to the witness having a copy of his report, even if it is tabbed and highlighted, I note from here I see some Post-It notes with some notes written on them. I would be interested to find out what that is and if the witness is relying on the same. I think I'm entitled to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have one Post-It where I talk about -- I mean, these are just -- I call it cheat sheets, but I can remove them if you want. I have one with dates where I have the dates of General Mladic's main military assignments since 1991. This is this one. There's one where I write down what situational awareness is, I can remove that. And then there is one where I have the distinction between -- sorry, in the command process and mainly the planning phase of the JNA or the SFRY armed forces, command forces, the distinction between the full procedure and the shortened procedure. But I have -- I mean, if Mr. Ivetic has a problem with these things, I can easily remove them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are two options. Either you remove them or you share the content with Mr. Ivetic as he asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can do both, actually. I mean, I need to remove them to share them with him, so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you are comfortable with that, then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we can do that and taking a break at the same time. Therefore, I would suggest that you give your Post-It notes to the usher who would then give them to Mr. Ivetic. I hope they're not in Flemish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, they're in English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, after you have been escorted out of the courtroom. No loud speaking. Mr. Mladic, no loud speaking, under no circumstances. That's the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break, and we will resume at ten minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be brought in, the 20 -- approximately 20 documents still to be tendered from the bar table in relation to Witness Treanor, could that be tendered as soon as possible. I noticed that the Defence, of course, has an opportunity to -- to add something to the table you are presenting. At the same time, it's the experience that often we found empty boxes there. So, therefore, we should avoid that we suffer any further delays in knowing what 20 documents or approximately 20 documents you would like to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it be convenient for the Court if it had Ms. Bibles here at the start of the next session this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it's filed this week, the Chamber will be happy. If that's not possible, then we'd like to hear why it is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I see on the transcript that already before you started speaking there is a little warning. If you could keep that in mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you just discussed the intelligence cycle methodology. Through the application of this methodology, how were you able to determine the reliability of information in documents?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was able to establish the reliability of information contained in documents by looking at different versions or different -- yeah, documents discussing the same event or similar events in order to establish what happened. Or -- to establish the facts related to a specific event or a specific issue or a specific situation. And then, of course, this is also linked. You have on the one hand the reliability of the source -- of the information -- yeah, you confused me because in the methodology you talk about the -- the reliability of the source and the credibility of the information. So that's why I started off wrongly. So you -- these are two different issues. In a nutshell, a reliable source can provide information of low credibility and vice versa. At face value it's, of course, difficult to say this is a reliable source or not or this information is credible or not. What you basically do, you look for corroboration. You look at the nature of the source, what is its relation with the event, what is the distance, does the source have a specific reputation. And then for the -- for the -- the -- the -- actual information, yeah, you look for other accounts or other -- or other sources that provide information on the event, and then you try to come to a common version. And I apologise for the length of the answer, but I was confused in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please scroll down on the page that is on the screen before us. And if we could please magnify the footnotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In footnote 3 on this page, it indicates that you've testified and applied the intelligence cycle methodology in all of the reports admitted in seven previous cases. Since the completion of the report for this case, did you testify as an expert witness on an eighth occasion in the Hadzic case?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 of this section which is on a previous page, you describe the scope of the report and indicate the report is an analysis of the role of Ratko Mladic as the deputy commander of the JNA 2nd Military District and commander of the VRS between early 1992 and November 1995. What types of materials did you rely upon to reach your conclusions as to Ratko Mladic's role?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- the -- the -- the materials I have used for this report I describe in detail in paragraph 4 of the scope of the report, but just to summarise, I -- I -- I considered main what I would call primary source, i.e., documents that were issued by the organisations, if I can call it that way, General Mladic belonged to during the relevant time-period. And obviously, I mean, this is the JNA, JNA 2nd Military District, command documents and reporting documents, the same for the VRS, and obviously in order to be able to understand them and to -- to -- to -- to see how he was exercising his authority, as that was one of the purposes of the report, I also looked at the doctrinal framework, i.e., what was the doctrine of these organisations, the JNA, the SFRY armed forces, the VRS, and that also involved looking at applicable legislation. For example, the constitution of the SFRY, of the FRY, of the SRBiH, and subsequently RS and other legislation that was relevant from a military point of view in order to understand how General Mladic exercised his authority in the positions he held in these two organisations, 2nd Military District and the VRS, and also what I call his situational awareness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt you right there, Mr. Theunens. In paragraph 2 of the same section, you describe the two parts of the report. I will ask you some more detailed questions about part 1 later today. However, at this time, could you please generally tell us why your analysis in part 1 is relevant to your conclusions concerning Ratko Mladic's role as commander of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- I believe I just -- I -- explained that in the sense that even if the VRS is officially created on the 12th of May, it is based on something that existed already and that something was organised and regulated in a particular manner. And in order to understand -- yeah, not only how the VRS would be organised and function, it wouldn't be sufficient to just have a few documents of the 2nd Military District but in my view it was essential to also look at what I call the doctrinal framework and the applicable legislation as I explained earlier, because, for example, when we talk somewhere about an operational group, well, I believe it would be helpful to explain what is an operational group. If we talk about a volunteer, I believed it would be helpful to explain, for example, the -- the legal conditions under which volunteers could join the armed forces. If we talk about orders that the VRS or General Mladic may have issued in relation to implementing the international laws of war, I believed it would be useful to look at the applicable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. -- Mr. Theunens, you are going, by far, too swiftly. And I see that parts of your testimony will be lost if you continue at that speed, which I like to prevent to happen. Please proceed. Mr. Weber will give you the right example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I hope so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, could you also check whether what we see on the transcript is one, but also listening to the other channels, there may be a serious problem there as well. So it's not only the transcript but also the other booth. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please just further explain, I believe that -- I don't know if you were going to cover this in your answer that you just stated. But why was the JNA's -- your analysis of the JNA's role in the conflict in Croatia relevant to your analysis of Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this analysis was relevant in my view because when you compare the two situations, i.e., on one hand, Croatia and, on the other hand, Bosnia-Herzegovina, the analysis I conducted allows to identify patterns not only in the way how the JNA, or subsequently the VRS, are being used, but also in relation to General Mladic, how he exercises his authority and -- and -- yeah, how he ensures his situational awareness. And I think that this continuity again in the context of my analysis is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You include summaries and introductory overviews at the beginning of each section of the different parts of your report. Do these summaries and overviews contain your analytical conclusions based on your review of available documentary material?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, it -- yes, Your Honours, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, the Prosecution requests that 65 ter 28612 be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I anticipate we will be making submissions after the witness's testimony from both sides, so I have no objection to it being marked for identification and reserve my arguments to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number under which it would be marked would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28612 receives number P3029, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, today I'm going to start by asking you a few general questions about Ratko Mladic and his style of command. I will then cover the topic of command and control discussed in part 1 of your report. After we address these matters, we will go through more specific topics an examples in documents. With this understanding, I would like to start by asking: Based on your review, could you please tell us whether Ratko Mladic was an active and involved military commander?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.
