Based on the review of the documents, those included in the report and also others, I would describe General Mladic as a very involved and a very active commander, who intervenes immediately when he feels or when he has the impressions that -- or maybe the chain of command has not been respected or when he believes that he has not been adequately informed by subordinates, and there are also numerous examples that instead of staying in the -- of staying in the headquarters, he moves to the area where the combat operations are being conducted not just by conducting visits but also by having forward command post established. And then the documents, I mean the VRS documents, show that he is actually actively leading these combat operations, and there are several examples of that as included in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Overall, would you consider Ratko Mladic to be a well-informed commander between 1991 and through 1995?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have less documents available for the time-period prior to the establishment of the VRS, but -- i.e., prior to -- and also General Mladic taking up the position of commander of the Main Staff of the VRS of the 12th of May, but for sure after 12th of May 1995 -- 1992, excuse me, until, say, November 1995, I would consider General Mladic as very well-informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Throughout part 1 of your report, you provide a detailed analysis of command and control doctrine as applied in the SFRY armed forces. In part 2 of your report, on pages 43, 66 to 67, and 163, among other, you conclude that command and control in the VRS is based on the same principles that apply to the SFRY armed forces. How did you reach this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I reached this conclusions by A, comparing the applicable legislation and regulations and; B, by analysing the various combat documents, be it command document or reporting documents, which often refer these -- the three principles of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For the record, the application of the SFRY doctrine by the VRS has also been mentioned by Witness Manojlo Milovanovic at page 16929 to 30 and Witness Dannatt at page 19138. On pages 36 to 40 of part 1, you explain the command structure of the JNA. In part 2 of your report, you discuss the structure of the VRS and you conclude on page 73 of part 2 that Ratko Mladic possessed the authority to order changes in the organisational structure of the VRS. Did Ratko Mladic organise the VRS and use a command structure similar to that of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, he did. There were, of course, some minor changes in relation to the structure in a sense that, whereas in a JNA unit you would have an assistant commander for political guidance, that person would be called assistant commander for religious and morale guidance in the VRS. And obviously whereas the JNA -- I mean, in the time of the SFRY armed forces there were two components - i.e., the JNA and the TO - when the VRS is established, the self-created Bosnian Serb TO in Bosnia-Herzegovina is integrated into the VRS. So once the VRS is fully organised, there is no Bosnian Serb TO anymore. But otherwise, there is a high degree of similarity both I would say at the staff level as well as at unit level in the -- in the structures of these two armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For the most part, did the VRS Main Staff's sectors fulfil similar duties as those organs in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm concerned that we're having leading question after leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this question is not leading. I'm just asking him if the VRS staff sectors fulfilled the same functions as in the former JNA. I'm asking him to explain, if he can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to say that there's no leading element in it at all would not be right, Mr. Weber. Could you try to -- having established that the structures were very similar, although it's small adaptations or small corrections, perhaps you could you can ask then whether the organs in the JNA and in the VRS Main Staff in their duties would show a similarity or not similarly. It's a matter of carefully phrasing. So if you would keep that in mind, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, did you just hear the Chamber's question?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I did, Your Honours. I already addressed the -- the -- the issue of -- of -- of political guidance versus morale and religious guidance. In addition, I also noted that whereas in the JNA or the SFRY armed force there was a separate security administration, and the functions of security intelligence indeed were separated. In the VRS Main Staff and the subordinate staffs, intelligence security are handled by one sector. So they are not separate but they are handled by one -- under the same sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Starting on page 12 to page 46 of part 1 of your report, you discuss command and control as defined by the JNA military lexicon, the JNA text on command and control, the All People's Defence law, and other military regulations. For us, right now, could you please tell us how does the SFRY armed forces define command and control?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, I will paraphrase the definition as it is provided in the corps regulation which states that command and control are conscious and organised activities of the commander in order to use the available means, be it personnel or resources, in the most effective manner to achieve the set goal. And these elements, i.e., conscious and organised, it is done by a commander, I mean, a single commander who has the exclusive right to command and control, and the use of resources, be it personnel or materiel, these elements we find in all references or definitions of command and control in SFRY armed forces doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us whether or not the command process is continuous?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It is continuous because obviously it will start sometime, i.e., when the unit starts, but once you have a unit, you have a commander, and in simple terms anything that happens in the military happens on orders. There may be -- there is something like initiative, but that has to be consistent with what is called in NATO the commander's intent. But otherwise, everything happens on orders. The commander issues orders and these go down through the chain of command, and the commander has to inform himself about the degree of implementation of these orders, and then, based on -- on his judgement, comparing the set task with the way in which it has been implemented, he can issue additional orders for corrective action or for small amendments. But this is a continuous cycle because, I mean, units are continuously acting, be it conducting operations or maintenance or training or any other activity personnel, military personnel is involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can a military commander exercise command without control?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, both SFRY armed forces or JNA regulations, as well as I copied US and UK regulations, emphasise that command and control are part of one and the same activity. You cannot exercise command without having control. So even if from maybe a semantic point of view one would be able to make a distinction between the two, from a practical military point of view they are part of one and the same activity by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You just mentioned US --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, I notice the witness keeps flipping back to a page that has more writing on it, and I'd like to see that page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Theunens. I think there were short annotations. If there's anything specifically which -- we're not going to give it right away to Mr. Ivetic. If you could explain what kind of assistance you find in your notes, then ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I use colours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And if the Trial Chamber is assisted by that, I can explain the -- the choice of colours to highlight certain elements. And then sometimes when I have like an article of -- of -- I mean, I'm trying to look at the page -- page with a lot of annotations. Okay. There is on page 12 of part 1 a title called: "Command and Control over the SFRY Armed Forces." I have added in handwriting within, i.e., the reference to the corps definition, that can be found on page 22. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page reference therefore.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, it's just for references. I mean -- a lot of page numbers, because I don't know this by heart, you know. When I worked here, I was fairly confident that I could find anything in my report, but the past four years have I been working on quite different matters. And even if I had a couple of days here to prepare myself, it is more challenging than it used to be to find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, satisfied?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am now satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just quickly, I do have a clean copy of the report if that is [Overlapping speakers] necessary, and also I did discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no need to provide the witness with a clean copy. The markings he made, Mr. Ivetic accepts them as being useful to be used during the examination of the witness, and we leave it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have been asked to convey a message from my client also. When dealing with portions of this rather lengthy report, if they could mention the page or paragraph number so they can be found in the B/C/S version of the same. So far, we've been using English page numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's, of course, one issue about what should be elicited viva voce and where we rely on the report, especially on part 1. Mr. Weber, you often introduce questions by look at this and this portion of the first part of the report where, of course, that is not the primary basis for eliciting the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just trying to provide transcript references so we can later associate and locate where the information is. And then I'm asking an additional question or questions based on the subject matter that is discussed on those pages. I, of course, can provide the e-court pages of both versions during any question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would. To the extent you are able to meet the request, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'm going to go back to the question I was about to ask you. You just mentioned US and UK regulations --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- do these regulations use a similar or different definition of command and control to that of the SFRY armed forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honour, these -- these definitions are included in pages 23 and subsequent in part 1 of the report, English version. And they have very similar to -- or I would almost say identical to the definitions used in SFRY armed forces doctrinal documents regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On pages 33 to 36 of part 1, available in e-court on English pages 68 to 71, and in B/C/S, on those same pages, you discuss how command and control process -- or excuse me, the command process and control is implemented through the functions of planning, organising, giving orders, co-ordination, and control, with inspection in parenthesis. I would like to briefly focus with you on this last function. Could you please tell us what is the control inspection function and how this is important to the exercise of command?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I just want to highlight that the use of the word "control" in this context is not to be confounded with the use of control in the context of command and control. And in B/C/S, the difference is very clear. The kind of control we are talking about now is called is "inspekcija" and other one is "rukovodjenje." But to answer the question, as I mentioned earlier it is not enough to issue an order. The commander also has to verify the degree of implementation of the order, and through inspection, as the -- as the text says, he can get an insight into the -- the status and degree of accomplishment of the tasks he has set in his order. And, again, I mean, the doctrine states these are continuous activities, and he basically, as I also said, you compare the set task with the actual result --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, should not speak aloud. It's the second or the third time today I have to remind him of that, and that is sufficient. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then through counsel you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Mladic is complaining that he's unable to follow the witness since again there has been no reference to page numbers in the B/C/S. And with the speed of the testimony, he is barely able to listen and to try to locate the sections of the report that might relate to the same discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But paragraph numbers are used repeatedly, I think. Let me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And they repeat throughout the report. I believe even page numbers in the different sections also recycle so that there are several page 12s, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, could you please keep in mind to be as clear as possible in your reference to portions of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will continue to now refer to the e-court pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 243 of part 2 of your report, which is in e-court English page 459 and B/C/S page 456, you conclude: "Ratko Mladic is systematically informed of the activities of his subordinate units and commands through regular operational reporting. He regularly visits and inspects commands and units, meets with commanders and, et cetera." You've commented on this already. How did this further General Mladic's ability to exercise control over his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, you mean control in the sense of the inspection function of command and control?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In carrying out the inspection function of command and control, how did this then more relate to his ability to exercise control in the sense of command and control? If that helps clarify.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I'm not -- I think I understand the question in the sense that by inspecting the units, and he can compare the task he has set with the actual situation on the ground, and that allows him to issue additional instructions to subordinate commanders if he -- if he feels as a commander that such additional orders are needed. And we have examples of that. So it is the regular implementation I would say of the command and control process as it is described in doctrine. Maybe with a difference that compared to -- to other commanding officers I have looked into during my time at ICTY, General Mladic was very active in that field. I mean, there's a whole range of visits and other meetings he conducts throughout the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina with units -- of units on the battle-field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On pages 31 to 33 of part 1, available in e-court in English on pages 66 to 68 and in B/C/S also on those same page, 66 to 68, you enumerate the seven principles of command and control. I would like to focus with you on three of these principles as they have been mentioned on numerous occasions during these proceedings but not fully defined. Could you please tell us what does the principle of single authority entail?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honour, single authority means that there is only one commander whereas the -- who has the exclusive right to issue orders and to whom the status of implementation of these orders has to be reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For the record, the principle of single authority has been mentioned during these proceedings at transcript pages 3174, 5017 to 18, 5127, 12579, 12811, 15679 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you check on the transcript whether all the pages you mentioned appear already. If not, to repeat if there's anything missing. And then slowly continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Continuing. Page 17277, 17417, and page 19062.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Turning to the next principle: What is the importance of the principle of subordination?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Subordination, Your Honours, means the obligation to implement the decision of a superior, and, as the regulations say, in an exact and timely manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For the record, the principle of subordination has been mentioned at transcript pages 2888 to 89, 2894, 4212, 5068, 11137, 11633, 11715, 12579, among other -- numerous other references. Continuing. Lastly, what is the principle of unity?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Unity, and I'm referring for this and the previous definitions to the 1983 [Realtime transcript read in error "1993"] JNA textbook on command and control, means that the defence of the country is integral and indivisible. And in practical terms, it means there is consistency between the orders of the Supreme Command, and those I mean directives, instructions, or other orders of the Supreme Command on one hand, and then orders and commands on the lowest level. Consistency in the contents and the overall purpose of these orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For the record, the principle of unity has been mentioned at transcript pages 2983, 3122, 3131, 4772, 5017 to 18, and 12883.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: And if you allow me just to small correction, it should be the 1983 JNA textbook on command and control. Not 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you. How does the application of these principles ensure that operations are conducted in accordance with commander's intended outcome?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, in practical term there is only -- there will be only one commander who can issue orders based on the singleness, the principle of singleness of command and control or single authority. Subordinates are obliged to implement these orders in a timely and exact manner. And throughout the chain of command, because, of course, the commander, he cannot issue orders to each individual soldier because through the principle of subordination a chain of command is established, and then -- I mean, all these orders would be consistent with -- with the commander's intent through the principle of unified command and control, and all the levels in the command and control system or in the chain of command are organised in a manner that allows for the implementation or the abidance by the three principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Since you've just mentioned a couple of different types of documents, I'd like to turn quickly with you, on pages 43 to 46 of part 1, which can be found in e-court in the English version and B/C/S version on pages 78 to 81. In your report on these page, you explain a different type of combat documents. Did the combat documents -- types of combat documents issued by or sent to Ratko Mladic and the VRS Main Staff, were they done in a similar manner or not as described by the SFRY military doctrine?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. For the two categories of combat document, i.e., first, command documents; and, secondly, reporting documents, we see the same types of documents on one hand in the SFRY armed forces and on the other hand in the VRS and for command documents the same hierarchy, and I guess you will come back to that, but that's explained in [indiscernible] pages of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just to break the two types of combat documents and discuss them a little further, what are the purpose of the command documents, like a directive or an order?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Command documents are issued to -- to -- yeah. To -- I want to say to issue commands but that would be too simple, but they are issued by the superior to issue tasks to the subordinates, and depending on the nature of these tasks, different categories exist. I mean, the highest level are the directives, subsequently we have instructions, then we have orders, and the lowest level of command document is a command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What are the purpose of notification documents, like reports?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Reports are intended to inform the commander of the degree of implementation of the set task. As -- again, this refers also to the -- to the control or the inspection function of -- of command and control, and the commander needs to know to what extent his tasks have been implemented, or he also needs to be informed of any other event or development that can be relevant for the tasks he has set.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 46 of part 1 of your report, which can be found in both versions in e-court at page 81, you explain the SFRY doctrine which requires a commander to "at all times know the status, position, and capabilities of his units two levels down." Could you please explain why such a requirement exists.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this -- this requirement follows from military structure and the hierarchy of units, i.e., starting from the top from the level of the VRS Main Staff. The commander of the VRS Main Staff will issue orders or will give tasks to his corps. Now, these corps, they consist of brigades, and it's actually the brigades -- it are actually the brigades of these corps that will do the task because the corps, it is just a staff and its subordinate units. So in order for the commander of the Main Staff to set the tasks of the corps, he needs to know the status of the units in the corps that will implement these tasks and these are the brigades. And the same system cascades down then because the brigade commander, on the basis of -- excuse me, corps commander on the basis of the orders from the commander of the Main Staff will issue tasks to -- to the brigade commanders, whereby, the corps commander needs to know the status of the battalions of these brigades. And then we go from brigade to battalion, and battalion to company. And this is how the system works.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If could you please in a little bit more detail explain how the regular reporting procedures of the VRS ensured that Ratko Mladic received information from at least two levels below him.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we look into the -- I mean, the regular and irregular reporting by the corps. There was daily reporting between May 1992 and -- and, say, November 1995, from the subordinate units to the superior units. The Main Staff, i.e., General Mladic, issued orders to the subordinate units to submit their daily reports or their regular reports in a timely fashion. I have seen a document where -- in which he issues instructions to subordinate commanders to call him, so that's an oral reporting. And there were also -- I mean, there were also procedures for irregular reporting in case of an unusual event where an urgent response was required as opposed to waiting for the dead-line set for the regular reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P3011, page 17 of the B/C/S and page 24 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The document that will be coming up before you is the SRBiH Law on Army dated 1 June 1992. You reference this document over 35 times throughout your report in relation to multiple topics. Today, I would like to focus with you on Article 173 which, I believe, in the English version, is at the bottom of the left column, continuing onto the top of the right column.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please zoom out the English version to see the full article.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Does this article incorporate the command and control principles of single authority, unity, and subordination?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It does, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We see that this is in chapter 11 of the Law on the Army, entitled: "Command." What does this indicate about how the VRS decided to incorporate these principles as part of their structure?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, it shows that the VRS applied the same principles in relation to command and control as the JNA, and I would say that these are -- these are universal principles. They applied to each armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of both versions of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I would like to briefly ask you about Article 10 under the chapter for replenishment of the army. Does this article bestow any authority to Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: In -- indeed, Your Honours, Article 10 explains the duties of the commander of the Main Staff. And they are enumerated there. There's also a reference in another article that the supreme commander can delegate certain authorities to the commander of the Main Staff. So I would say have you to look at Article 10 in conjunction with Article 174 of the -- this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We've mentioned five functions of the command process already in your report. Do the powers in this article that is before us relate to any of those five functions?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, they do, Your Honours. Most obviously you have planning and organising, but that will, of course, also imply co-ordination, command, and an inspection, as usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about do start on another rather lengthy document. If we could take the break at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can take a break now. Could we first ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Mr. Weber, I make one observation. In our decision on the evidence of Mr. Theunens, and I'm specifically referring to the decision of the 18th of October, we said: "Having reviewed the unredacted portions, the Chamber's position is still that part 1 is excessive in length in light of its apparent limited relevance. The Chamber would therefore prefer that the Prosecution elicit any relevant matters related to part 1 during the examination of Mr. Theunens." Now, I'm seeing that you are doing your utmost best to do that. At the same time, there is frequent reference to sometimes longer portions of the report. Now, if you would elicit that evidence without such references, you could then redact the report in such a way that you can understand the evidence without having looked at the report. So instead of saying, In paragraph so-and-so you deal with this and this and this, can you explain a little bit further on what you mean there. That is a way of proceeding which would still require for us to look at those portions of the report, although you elicited some of the evidence viva voce. That is of some concern, and you should be aware that if the Chamber has clearly expressed that it is still excessive in length, that if you refer to, at the very end, many, many portions of the already redacted part 1, that you might get into trouble. I just want to draw your attention to that at this moment. For example, if I say, I would like that ask you five questions about command and control in comparing US or UK command and control with VRS command and control, could you point at some differences. Then we -- there's no reference to the report anymore, and we would receive that evidence viva voce. Therefore, the mixed way of operation is not without some concern and is perhaps also not without risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in preparations, again, it's been very difficult with the Chamber's guidance, and I understand your concern. On the other hand, Your Honour, we need to get this evidence in, these definitions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We said something about the limited relevance. If you say we have to get it in, you are more or less ignoring what the Chamber said. If you say in preparation it has been very difficult with the Chamber guidance, that is an observation which may express that you are not fully observing that guidance, which is not a very good thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to be the utmost respectful to the Chamber's guidance. I hope Your Honour is aware of that. On the other hand, I -- I'm a bit perplexed, I guess would be a more neutral way of saying this, that whether or not the Chamber is saying that they find of limited relevance command and control -- the notions of command and control in a military case involving Ratko Mladic not to be -- or to be of limited relevance, and this a key part of the Prosecution's case, and I don't know want to go to the point where I'm simply asking Mr. Theunens to read definitions on the record because I know you can read those. However, they're clearly in the report and in the text. So I'm trying to achieve a balance, and I know we're going to take a break right now. I'll be guided by Your Honours, but I'm trying to be mindful of many different considerations here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if you say, I'm -- that we can read them, that means: Read the report. And the guidance was: Select carefully from the report what is really vital, elicit that viva voce, and then -- and observations like makes no use because you can read the report to some extent ignores the guidance of the Chamber. I took, as a starting point, your reference to sometimes major parts, many, many pages of the report. There is a way of eliciting the vital elements of that evidence without referring to many, many pages of the report. I leave it to that. Please consider it over the break. Perhaps discuss it with your colleagues. And we'll resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you may have misunderstood me. I didn't say that command and control is not relevant. Not at all. Focused questions on command and control, 15, 20, 25, bring you to the core of the command and control issue instead of 900 -- 180 pages. That's the issue. It's the level of detail. It is the excessive length of the explanations, and the details are not of such relevance that they justify so many pages. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the Prosecution please have P338, page 8 of the B/C/S and page 7 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: While this document is coming up, Mr. Theunens, could you please generally describe the scope and purpose of the 1992 combat readiness report that was completed in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the VRS analysis of the combat readiness covering 1992 provides a detailed insight in the way how the VRS was established, as well as is how -- I mean, for the different aspects of the armed forces, and in addition, it also provides a detailed analysis on obviously the combat readiness, the current state of the armed forces, and how they have been operating so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before you is the first section of the 1992 combat readiness report. I would like to direct your attention to the fourth paragraph from the top of this page. The one that begins with the reference to the fact: "We have carried out individual and concerted battle operations according to a single design and plan ..." Based on your review of materials, what was the overall single strategic plan that was implemented by Ratko Mladic and the VRS in 1992?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on -- on the review of the document I had available to me, I considered the six strategic goals as the main political or strategic guidance determining the operations of the VRS not only in 1992 but until the end of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The remainder of this paragraph discusses the temporary grouping of forces into operational groups, tactical groups, and combat groups. This is something that you deal with on pages 57 and 60 of Part 1 in your report. For the record, if you can just please define for us what an operational group is first.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, an operational group is an ad hoc formation that can consist of several brigades operating under a single and unified command, that conduct operations in a specific area during a specific time-period. The relevance of the establishment of an ad hoc formation relies or resides in the fact that an operational group will include units of different backgrounds, i.e., different JNA units. You can have brigades from different corps. But in the context that we're talking here, and mainly what we saw in Croatia, operational groups allowed to establish single command and control over JNA units, local Serb TO units, units of the TO Serbia, local Serb police units, as well as volunteers/paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to what you say a tactical group is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, a tactical group applies the same principles. However, on a lower level, i.e., a tactical group would consist of -- of battalion-level units. And, again, there is some room for maneuver because on one hand there is the doctrine, but on the other hand there are the examples that we see during the conflict in Croatia in the latter. But on the other hand, there are the examples we see during the conflict in Croatia during the latter half of 1991 where the JNA establishes, I mean, regularly establishes operational groups, tactical groups, as well as assault detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to how the VRS used OGs and TGs, and I would just note for you on page 43 of Part 2 of your report, you conclude: "Throughout the conflict the VRS established OG and TG in order to ensure single unified and uninterrupted command and control over all forces conducting combat operations." Could you please more specifically explain how the VRS used these formations to ensure single authority and unified command.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, whenever the commander saw a need to establish such a temporary formation, because he may have received units belonging to different establishment units or there could be cases where units of the police were involved, then he could decide to establish such an ad hoc temporary formation, and then we would have to have look at the specific orders as well as, I mean, command documents and reporting documents to see where such OGs or TGs operated and how they functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Returning to the combat analysis report that's before you and directing your attention to the next paragraph which is the fifth from the top, it refers to how unity was achieved by following well-known principles that had a crucial bearing on command and control in the VRS. Does this paragraph again confirm that the VRS was in fact using the SFRY principles of command and control which you discuss throughout Part 1 of your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. These principles are the same as those listed or identified by SFRY armed forces doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There's a reference in this document to the principle of operational ability and security.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you could please assist us and explain what that principle is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: For the sake of time I just paraphrase them, but operability or operational ability means that the system has to be adopted to the specific conditions, because when combat operations are being conducted, there may be a high tempo with -- with swift changes in who controls which area. Units may change and so on, so the command and control system has to be able to manage those changes. And security is what we would call now operational security, i.e., that confidentiality of information is maintained and that, for example, adequate communication systems are available to -- to -- to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please scroll down on the page before us. In the following paragraph, which is the fourth -- or excuse me, the second from the bottom, there's reference to offensive and defensive actions. In preceding paragraph, we saw reference to how the VRS carried out its operations pursuant to a single design and plan. Based on these references, at this time could you please explain to us the difference between strategy and tactics?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: You mean in the context of how the VRS operated?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I guess maybe let's break it down a little bit more. In general, could you explain to us, first, what is strategy; and then, secondly, what are tactics.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, strategy refers to, I would say, the general political guidance on how -- excuse me, on which goals the armed forces should pursue. And then tactics, I mean, is at the other end because we do not discuss at the operational level, but tactics are the basic principles as to how armed force act. I mean, various concepts, type of operations they undertake or actions they undertake in the framework of this overall strategy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At what level of command are strategic decisions made in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: At -- Your Honours, at the level of -- of the Main Staff? You can find in my report, I have the -- the -- the SFRY armed forces had the definitions for the levels of command: The strategic level, the operational level, the tactical. And there it sets the strategic level includes the main -- excuse me, the Supreme Command and the staff of the Supreme Command. And you will see that in the analysis of the combat readiness report, there is an entry stating that the Main Staff operated as the staff of the Supreme Command. So this illustrates that strategic decisions are taken by the Main Staff on the basis of the political guidance given by the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You just made a reference as to where we could find something in your report. If there's any way could you tell us where that is, and then if you could just help us by explaining maybe in a little more detail how the SFRY armed forces define the strategic level --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Mm-hm --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- then the operational level and then so forth.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It's on English page 15. I don't have B/C/S references. And this is taken from a 1983 JNA manual for the work of commands and staffs. It's footnote 35 of Part 1 of the report. And I think it is pretty obvious, but the levels are defined. There have been changed over time; for example, I think the operational level makes mention here of armies but armies were replaced by Military District at the end -- Military Districts at the end of the 1980s and the division is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I appreciate it might be clear on the page, Mr. Theunens, but actually could you please first explain under the 1983 JNA manual what -- what the strategic level is and what their responsibilities are?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I will repeat myself to a certain extent but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, were you informed by the Prosecution about the discussion the Chamber had with the Prosecution about how to present your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- you mean the discussions in September Your Honours or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. About the length of your explanations and that the Chamber urged the Prosecution to elicit as much as possible viva voce evidence. Therefore, if you say, I repeat myself, what we are seeking is a condensed evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and that is the reason why Mr. Weber now and then will ask questions where you may be surprised because they're already in your report. But the level of detail of the report is such that the Chamber, especially if it is about the general overview rather than the events on the ground, is seeking to have condensed, succinct evidence. So don't worry if you repeat yourself but then -- in approximately perhaps 10 per cent of the time or the number of words to be used for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I understand, Your Honours, and your clarification is -- is very helpful. Strategic level is the Supreme Command and that was in the time of SFRY, the SFRY Presidency. And, of course, that also then includes the Supreme Command staff which at the time was the SSNO, the Secretariat for All People's Defence. The operational level is the military command level below the Supreme Command Staff. At that time in 1983 were armies but those are in fact the Military Districts. And, of course, it also includes the corps commands as well as equivalent TO commands, i.e., republican and provincial TO command. And then the tactical level is anything below so from the division downwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You've already mentioned in the VRS at what level the strategic decisions were made. Could you tell us now at what level of command would the operational and tactical decisions made in the VRS -- what levels, plural.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, the Main Staff and obviously the commander of the Main Staff is responsible for translating political guidance military goals or military tasks, and this is the strategic/operational level. For me, the corps command also includes the operational level, but I think it's a matter of semantics, and anything below the corps, i.e., brigades, battalions, and equivalent units, up to the squad level is the tactical level.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for those explanations. Could the Prosecution please have the next page of Exhibit P338. In the first full paragraph from the top of this page, the report describes how decisions were made on the engagement of VRS forces at Main Staff meetings headed, as a rule, by the commander, with the active participation of other officers. In the course of this explanation, there's reference to the so-called full method and other methods. First, could you please explain what the full method is, according to SFRY military doctrine.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- the full method for the implementation of command and control process -- or the command process which means that all staff sections, so not only the commander and the assistant commanders but also the members of the staff, are consulted in order to transform the task received from the Superior Command into orders for the subordinate units. The commander will consult with everybody but, of course, he has the -- the freedom, as he is the commander, to decide himself to what extent he will make use of the result of these consultations and how -- I mean, the actual, his decision, will be. Or what his decision will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There is also reference to another method, the fast-track method. Could you please explain this method to us. How it differs from the full method.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, what is here described, Your Honours, as fast-track method is in the doctrine described as the shortened method. And it means that the commander will only consult with his assistant commanders, or even he will not consult, and then he comes to a decision. The -- the -- the reasons -- I mean, the main criteria for the choice -- for choosing are obviously the available time. If the commander has a lot of time available, then he will most likely choose for the full method. If there is not a lot of time available, and by "time available," I mean, okay, between receiving the task from the superior command and the moment he and his units have to be ready to implement that task. So if there's not enough time available, then he will choose for the shortened method. Or the fast-track method, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please scroll down on this page. In the second paragraph from the bottom, there's a discussion of command posts and the development of their infrastructure. If I could just refer you to pages 42 and 43 of Part 1 of your report, where you describe command posts, their purpose, and the various types. Could we just please just go step by step with this. Could you first explain under JNA doctrine what are the purpose of command posts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- a command post is the geographic location from where command and control are exercised. Or, sorry, "exercises" is a French word. Are implemented. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just, Mr. Theunens, go ahead. And if you have to give more complete explanations, I -- I see that there's are number of other items that you might think are clear on this page. But do command posts consist under the -- of appropriate communications centres?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, they do, Your Honours. Because, as I said, command posts are the geographic location from where command and control are exercised. We have seen the seven principles of command and control. Continuity is one of these principles, so the location and the facilities available at that location for the command post must allow to implement uninterrupted command and control. Command and control involves that orders are issued but also that reports are received. And this done through communication assets, which can be couriers but, I mean, as we see from the documents, telex, for example, telephone, and in those times -- I mean, telex and telephone in those times were -- are the main communication assets, together with radios. What -- what is important -- what I consider important in the context of the report is the concept of a forward command post --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, sorry to interrupt you. I'm going to have to go step by step through each of these.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I know it's written there, but ... You -- you discuss the different -- six different types of command posts. If we could just go one by one, and I note these descriptions are straightforward, but if could you please include a short but comprehensive explanation on them. What ask a basic command post?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Well, usually in military documents, the basic command post is identified as the command post, i.e., the location from where command and control are implemented. Whether it's during an exercise or during combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, I'm just going to have go through this a little bit more with you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At what levels of command are basic command posts established?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I mean, they're established at -- at all levels. Obviously a platoon will not have a command post because a platoon is -- I mean, in the kind of operations we're talking about, be it infantry, or armour, they -- if they have -- the commander will be in his vehicle or on the terrain and that's from where he and maybe an assistant with a radio will exercise command and control. A company may have several vehicles. And then, when we go higher, indeed, a corps -- I'm jumping a few levels. But from brigade, division, corps, they will have fixed command posts which can be located in buildings or in tents or in -- in trucks. I mean, any facility that allows to -- that to exercise command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just to finish off this definition, is it -- is it accurate that according to the JNA doctrine that the location of the command post is placed to ensure successful command and control without frequent change of position?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And I should have said that. It's always a challenge between finding a location that is close enough to where the action takes place but, at the same time, it has to be secure. And if we are involved in mobile operations, then the command post may have to change from time to time, not just because of the range of the radios or -- or of communication lines but also of security. If you're too close to the confrontation line, then you expose yourself. And this is one of the reasons why, in highly mobile operations, forward command posts with be established. And that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Okay. Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The second one that you have in your report here is a logistics command post. Could you please tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It's -- we apply the same principles, Your Honours, but it is to -- to -- to organise. I mean, to command and control logistic support, be it supply, maintenance, evacuation of casualties, and so on. And this is usually separated from the command post which deals mainly with operational issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just to proceed maybe a little bit more quickly for the end of the day. Is it correct that logistics command posts are set up by commands of a higher level than those of basic command posts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I -- I -- it's not entirely correct. I mean, I cannot say in the JNA I -- at what level logistic command posts were set up. I mean, from my own experience, in -- in -- in our armed forces -- a battalion doesn't have a separate logistic command post, but all the logistic report will be separate. More in the rear, because -- I mean, they're more vulnerable, and there is no requirement for them to be close to the confrontation line. And it's -- it's a huge thing because if you have a mechanized unit, I mean, spare starts, ammunition and all those things take a lot of space. So, for a battalion, what we call it the trains. I don't know how it was called in the JNA because I didn't look so much in that aspect of logistic support. But, for sure, I would say from a brigade level and corps looking at the sheer size of the infrastructure that is needed, and I think that is it also illustrated when you look at, for example, the statements of General Mladic in relation to consumption of ammunition and the support required from VJ, there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm sorry, Your Honours. There, obviously you will have a separate logistics command post to manage and -- I mean, to command and control basically those aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what is a forward command post or IKM?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Forward command posts are established when there are operational requirements to do so, i.e., when there is a highly mobile operation, and/or when it is difficult to exercise command and control from the regular command post because of the terrain, because of other factors. Forward command posts are much smaller and they really include the essential parts of the command posts in order conduct the operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At what level of commands are forward command posts established?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: I would say, for sure, starting at the level of brigade and then upwards. Brigade, division, and corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did -- during the course of VRS operations, did the Main Staff, and in particular, Mr. Mladic, set up Main Staff forward command posts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, for a number of -- what I considered key operations, forward command posts were set up. They could have been set up by the Main Staff or by the units conducting the operations obviously on the orders of the Main Staff, and General Mladic would exercise command and control from these forward command posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to skip the reserve command posts and go onto the command posts referred on page 43 of Part 1 of your report. Could you please tell us what a joint command post is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, this is the doctrine as it is stated there. It is when there are both JNA and TO operating. Now, when I look at the practical situation, as it was in Croatia, given the -- or -- Croatia. Or Bosnia-Herzegovina. Given the developments in relation to the TO, there was -- no such joint command posts were established for the operations I have reviewed. There were just the command posts which were mainly manned by JNA personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just briefly, could you tell us what a false command post is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, the doctrine says it is part of operational camouflage activity, i.e., it's deception. It is to deceive the enemy about the location of the command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, perhaps this is two examples. Is there any false command post actively involved in this case? For the previous one, the witness told us that no joint command posts were established. Of course, we are aware of command posts. We are aware of forward command posts because that's part of the evidence. Why do we have to know what kind of command posts could have been used in other circumstances elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd say the fact that joint command posts were not necessary and were not needed is relevant to the fact that the VRS didn't need to set up such command posts. And we will return to some examples and concepts related to this later on when discussing the examples. I wasn't just -- I was asking particularly for the reason, the fact that the VRS did not use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. And the false command posts, same?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There may be reference to them. But I -- I -- that's why I asked briefly, just for completion. I will keep it in mind. I understand what Your Honour is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you a little bit about the SFRY doctrine of All People's Defence or ONO. This is discussed throughout Part 1 of your report on numerous pages. I'll try to direct you to the -- to specific ones as they come up. Could you please tell us what the SFRY doctrine of All People's Defence is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this doctrine means that all available resources, be it human or materiel, are used in defence -- to defend the country against an aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, where does the concept of All People's Defence originate from?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It was introduced in 1969, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How? Mr. Theunens, I know this is in your report, but if could you please specify as much information as possible.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think -- I mean, then I haven't seen the documents from 1969. But given the other documents, that is when, based on the -- how -- the then-President Tito and other senior officials saw the situation in -- in the countries surrounding Yugoslavia, that they considered it important to introduce this doctrine. And then after that, obviously subsequent doctrinal documents are developed, and we see the establishment of -- of -- of TO units on the various levels by republic, by -- and later on also for the autonomous provinces when those are created and that cascades down to -- to the lower level, in order to, indeed, allow the population, in addition to materiel resources, to participate in the defence the country. In addition to the -- the usual armed forces, if I can express myself that way, which was the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How does the All People's Defence doctrine incorporate the command and control principles of single authority and unity?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: It does, Your Honours, by explaining, for example, when I cited earlier the definition of command and control as it is mentioned in the 1990 corps regulation, it states that when JNA and TO are active in the same area that then command and control is in the hands of the commander of the operations, i.e., there will always be one commander. Again, for what we saw during the conflict in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to the establishment of the VRS, it is the JNA officer who is in command of operations. Remember what I said about OGs involving TO. But theoretically there can be situations where a TO commander can be in command of JNA forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Whenever it's good for Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. It's quarter part 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we'd like to see you back on Thursday, so we're not sitting tomorrow. We'll not finish on Thursday. But, just, that's the first day when we'd like to see you back at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, II. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, and I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way, with whomever, about your testimony, whether already given, or still to be given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume, Thursday, the 5th of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 5th day of December, 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 25
